children: From leading CEAT’s transformation to shaping RPG Group’s long-term strategy, Anant Goenka, Vice Chairman, RPG Group discusses professional management, capital allocation, the Camso acquisition and more

You moved from operating roles within RPG to leading CEAT and becoming Group Vice Chairman in 2023. What decisions are directly under your mandate today, and how are responsibilities divided between you, Harsh Goenka and the professional CEOs?

My role today is very different from what it was when I was running CEAT. As CEO, I was deeply involved in execution and operational decisions. At the Group level, I focus on shaping our long-term direction and enabling our businesses to build for the future. I work closely with our companies on strategy, leadership recruitment and development, the Group’s values and culture, digital transformation, innovation, excellence and sustainability.
One lesson I learnt at CEAT is that a CEO can get consumed by the pressures of the current quarter. As Vice Chairman, I have the opportunity to spend more time thinking about the longer term.

While RPG Group is promoter-led, we believe in empowering professional leaders. The CEOs and management teams are accountable for business performance, execution and day-to-day decisions. Harsh Goenka, as Chairman, provides the overall vision, values and stewardship, while I work alongside him on strategic priorities and the next phase of growth.
My accountability is to strengthen the Group’s long-term performance and relevance while preserving its values, governance and people-centric culture.

During your tenure as MD & CEO, CEAT’s market capitalisation rose 25-fold, alongside WEF Lighthouse recognition and the Deming Grand Prize. Which strategic decision you drove had the biggest impact on CEAT’s business and economics?

If I had to identify one decision, it would be committing CEAT to a long-term journey of quality and customer-centricity. We chose to build the organisation around the TQM framework, or Total Quality Management. This entailed robust business processes, continuous improvement, and employee ownership and involvement, rather than treating quality as a manufacturing initiative alone. Over the years, this approach has become deeply entrenched in the company’s culture.

This foundation allowed us to embrace digital technologies, improve productivity, accelerate innovation and consistently deliver better products to customers. It strengthened our credibility with OEMs, supported our move into premium segments, helped expand our presence in international markets and enabled us to offer greater value to our stakeholders.

The impact on the economics of the business was significant. Better quality, stronger brand preference and higher operational efficiency reinforced one another, creating a more resilient and profitable growth model. Recognitions such as the Lighthouse designation and the Deming Grand Prize were outcomes of this journey.
How do you influence Group strategy while preserving management accountability, and what major decision have you personally shaped?
The biggest adjustment in moving from CEO to Vice Chairman is understanding that influence is often more effective than authority.
When I was running CEAT, I could make decisions directly. At the Group level, my role is often to ask the hard questions, challenge assumptions and help our leaders think differently about a problem.
One Group-level decision I have helped shape is the adoption of the Total Quality Management approach across all our companies.

I have learnt that professional management works best when accountability remains clear. If the Group starts making every decision, accountability gets diluted. The objective is to provide perspective, challenge and support, while allowing operating teams to own the outcomes.
That is also how I was developed as a leader. I was given opportunities to learn, make mistakes and grow. I believe the same principle applies across the organisation.
How has RPG’s 70:20:10 capital allocation translated into actual investments, which venture is closest to becoming material, and what determines whether you scale or exit?
Our approach is to strengthen the Group’s core businesses while selectively investing in adjacencies and emerging areas aligned with long-term trends.

Taabi, TyresNMore and Asvata help us address new customer needs, test business models and build future capabilities. Each is at a different stage, so it is too early to judge them purely by scale or revenue.

We focus on whether a venture solves a meaningful customer problem and builds a sustainable market position. Strong customer adoption, sound unit economics and strategic relevance will determine whether we continue investing. Our aim is to build the Group’s next generation of growth opportunities while maintaining capital discipline.
What role did you play in CEAT’s Camso acquisition, and what growth and return benchmarks will define its success?

The Camso acquisition is particularly meaningful because it brings together many of the themes that have shaped CEAT’s journey over the last decade. While evaluating the opportunity, our focus was on assessing Camso’s potential to accelerate CEAT’s global ambitions. What made Camso attractive was its combination of a premium brand, access to new customer segments, strong global OEM relationships and a culture that places tremendous emphasis on quality. In many ways, we saw an alignment between CEAT’s own quality journey and the heritage Camso had developed under Michelin.

Ultimately, the success of the acquisition will be judged by whether it places CEAT in a stronger position. We should see growth in the business, improving profitability as integration progresses, and returns that justify the capital invested. Equally important will be our ability to expand customer relationships, strengthen our presence in premium segments and markets, and establish CEAT as a more significant global player in off-highway mobility.
How do you ensure RPG’s “Hello Happiness” philosophy drives measurable gains in productivity, innovation, retention and profitability?

Hello Happiness stems from a simple belief: people perform at their best when they feel trusted, valued, heard and connected to a larger sense of purpose. In any organisation, sustainable performance ultimately comes from people who care deeply about what they do and feel empowered to make a difference.

That is why we have worked to make the philosophy measurable and actionable. Through our Happiness Framework, annual Happiness Survey, employee-listening mechanisms and leadership practices, we seek to understand what enables people to thrive and do their best work. The outcomes we track go beyond satisfaction levels to include retention, leadership development, collaboration, digitisation, innovation and the overall strength of our talent pipeline.

In my experience, the link between employee wellbeing and business performance is quite direct. Teams that feel heard and empowered tend to solve problems faster, demonstrate a greater sense of ownership, invest more effort in creating customer delight and embrace change more readily. Over time, these behaviours show up in productivity, innovation and business performance. That is why we see Hello Happiness as both a people philosophy and an important contributor to long-term organisational success.
What is India’s biggest manufacturing constraint, and which RPG business could become a global category leader over the next decade?

India has all the ingredients to become a global manufacturing powerhouse. What we need now is a consistent focus on building world-class capabilities in quality, innovation, productivity and supply-chain resilience. Over time, excellence in these areas will help Indian companies earn the trust of customers worldwide and become global leaders in their categories.

Within RPG, CEAT is well positioned to play that role. Over the last decade, the company has invested deeply in quality, manufacturing excellence, technology and brand building. More recently, its expansion in specialty tyres and the Camso acquisition have strengthened its global footprint and opened up new growth opportunities.
